\subsection{The codec ladder}

Table~\ref{tab:main} reports the full ladder and Table~\ref{tab:head} the paired
head-to-head differences. Every interval in Table~\ref{tab:head} excludes zero.

\paragraph{The earlier result reproduces, and then reverses.} Against the
uniform-codebook control the polar code is ahead, exactly as the earlier draft
reported: $+0.019776$ versus $+0.022607$. Against the matched control it is
behind. Repairing the polar assignment rule and fitting its radius grid recovers
part of the gap but does not close it. The conclusion of
Section~\ref{sec:ceiling} therefore survives the move from weight MSE to
held-out loss, which is not automatic: this project has repeatedly found that
weight-error rankings fail to predict task rankings.

\paragraph{The result also survives the earlier draft's own selection rule.}
The ladder above selects each layer's pairing by activation-weighted error. The
earlier draft instead selected by calibration NLL, screening each layer against
an otherwise-BF16 model. Tables~\ref{tab:fair} and \ref{tab:fairhead} grant that
rule to every codec, with the codecs that can use activation statistics
receiving the identical BF16-measured statistic, so that selection effort and
activation information are no longer confounded with codec choice. Polar reaches
$+0.015902$ while the matched scalar control reaches $+0.008539$, a paired
difference of $+0.007364$ $[+0.006332,+0.008376]$. That control value is also
below the earlier draft's published polar figure of $+0.009333$, so the headline
comparison reverses even taken at face value.

\input{fairness_table.tex}

\paragraph{The earlier draft's calibration size does not discriminate, and we
say so.} That draft used four calibration windows (512 tokens) with a fixed
seed. On that seed the matched control wins comfortably, $+0.007609$ against
polar's $+0.011358$. Repeating with two further calibration seeds shows the
protocol is not decisive: over three seeds polar averages
$0.010945\pm0.000422$ and the matched control $0.010554\pm0.003349$, and on one
seed the control loses outright. Its seed-to-seed spread is eight times larger,
because its clip-factor search is a finer decision than polar's four-way pairing
choice and 512 tokens cannot resolve it.

We therefore do \emph{not} rest the conclusion on this protocol. It rests on
the 16-window comparisons, where the statistics are adequately estimated and the
matched control wins under both selection rules ($+0.014717$ against
$+0.019776$, and $+0.008539$ against $+0.015902$). What the 4-window sweep does
establish is narrower but still relevant: all three of our polar draws fall in
$[+0.010515,+0.011358]$, so the earlier draft's published $+0.009333$ lies
outside the spread we could reproduce and is best read as a fortunate draw from
a high-variance selector.

\paragraph{The pairing idea survives the parameterization that motivated it,
but does not clearly beat a well-tuned scalar code.} Under the single protocol
of Table~\ref{tab:fair}, the activation-weighted 256-point 2-D codebook gives
the best point estimate of any codec we tested, $+0.007693$. It carries the same
four index bits per weight and one FP32 row scale; its 2\,KB per-tensor codebook
is $0.065\%$ of that tensor's payload. Two of its three comparisons are
conclusive and one is not, and we report the distinction rather than eliding it:

\begin{itemize}
\item It beats polar decisively, $+0.008210$ $[+0.007205,+0.009186]$.
\item Activation weighting is what makes the difference: the unweighted 2-D
 codebook is worse by $+0.001452$ $[+0.000556,+0.002327]$. This matters for
 Section~\ref{sec:scffail}, because it is the same statistics-sensitivity that
 the self-consistent loop exploits.
\item Against the matched scalar control the paired difference is $+0.000846$
 with interval $[-0.000169,+0.001822]$, which \emph{includes zero}.
\end{itemize}

We therefore do not claim a settled advantage for the 2-D codec over a
well-tuned scalar code at this budget. The defensible claim is asymmetric: the
2-D codec reaches the scalar code's regime and may exceed it, while the polar
code is significantly behind both.

\subsection{Self-consistent calibration}
\label{sec:scffail}

We ran the SCF loop in two configurations. The first shares sixteen calibration
windows (2{,}048 tokens) between the statistics estimate and the energy guard.
The second estimates statistics on 64 windows and evaluates the guard on a
\emph{disjoint} 64 windows from the same training split.

\paragraph{The shared-window configuration fails, and the churn statistic says
why.} With the guard evaluated on the windows that produced the statistics,
every codec's calibration energy falls below its one-shot value -- and the 2-D
codec's held-out loss \emph{rises}, from $+0.009789$ to $+0.012509$. The scalar
and polar codecs are unaffected to within noise.

The assignment-churn statistic explains the pattern, and its ordering is the
same in both configurations. Table~\ref{tab:scf} reports the second one: at the
loop's last iteration the scalar codec has moved $3.2\times10^{-5}$ of its
assignments, because the statistics enter it only through a per-row clip choice;
the polar codec $8.1\times10^{-4}$; the 2-D codec $0.33$. In the first
configuration the corresponding figures are $5.4\times10^{-4}$,
$6.8\times10^{-5}$ and $0.28$. \emph{The loop changes a codec in
proportion to how much that codec's decisions actually depend on the activation
statistics.} That sensitivity is the point of the method, and it is also exactly
what lets the 2-D codec overfit a 2{,}048-token statistic.

This is a limitation of the guarantee, not a violation of it. The monotonicity
proved in Section~\ref{sec:scq} is monotonicity in \emph{calibration} loss, and
a guard evaluated on the fitting data cannot detect a step that improves only
the fitting data.

\paragraph{Separating the statistics from the guard repairs it.} With 64
windows for the statistics and a disjoint 64 for the guard, the loop improves
every codec it moves at all:

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{lrrr}\toprule
Codec & One-shot & With SCF & Change\\\midrule
real-4, Lloyd & $+0.014717$ & $+0.014717$ & $0$\\
polar, repaired & $+0.015206$ & $+0.014860$ & $-0.000346$\\
paired 2-D & $+0.009568$ & $\mathbf{+0.008983}$ & $-0.000585$\\\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Three things are worth noting. First, the $+0.012509$ regression becomes a
$-0.000585$ improvement purely by changing what the guard is evaluated on --
the statistics mixing itself was never the problem. Second, the scalar code's
result is \emph{identical} to its one-shot value to six decimals: the guard
rejected all five trial steps (Table~\ref{tab:scf}) and the loop fell back
exactly on one-shot calibration. That is the safe-drop-in property behaving as designed, and it is
the correct answer for a codec whose decisions barely depend on the statistics.
Third, the improvement ordering again tracks statistics-sensitivity, now in the
useful direction.

\paragraph{What is and is not claimed.} The self-consistency gap is real and
measurable: after one iteration the quantized model's activation statistics
differ from the BF16 model's by a relative residual of $0.5$--$2.2\%$ on these
projections, and the one-shot calibration every activation-aware quantizer
performs is fitted to the wrong one. Closing that gap is worth $-0.000585$ NLL
for the codec most able to exploit it, which is small but free of any change to
model size, format, or decode cost, and costs one forward pass per iteration
with no backward pass. It requires enough calibration data to estimate the
target statistics and a guard set that did not produce them; without both, it
makes things worse. We regard the diagnostic -- assignment churn predicts both
the benefit and the overfitting risk -- as the more transferable finding.
